input.question: How Small Would Something Have to be in Order to Orbit Around Someone in Space?
input.ground_truth: There is no mass limit, but both the person and other object orbit the center of mass of the system. For a very light object, the center of mass will be inside the person. For heavier and heavier objects, the center of mass will gradually move farther toward the other object, until for equal mass the point is exactly in the middle. [Watch these animations](_URL_1_) to see what I mean. Based on the masses and distances of the objects, speed is the critical quantity. To orbit a 100 kg person 1 meter away circularly, a small object should move at about [80 microns/s](_URL_0_), or 1 orbit every 21.4 hours.

Okay! Imagine you have a tiny marble and you're holding a big ball in space. If you let go of the marble, it will just float away, right? But if you throw the marble really, really gently so it doesn't go too fast or too slow, it might go around the big ball instead of flying away or falling straight in.

Now, how small the marble can be doesn't really matter—it could be a tiny pebble or a little grain of sand. What matters is how you throw it! But there's a catch: if the marble is so tiny that even a little bit of sunlight or a bump from another tiny thing in space pushes it away, it might not stay in orbit for long.

But if you could protect it and throw it just right, even something super, super small—like a speck of dust—could go around the big ball in space, as long as it moves at the right speed and doesn’t hit anything else.

So, the size doesn’t have to be big at all! It just has to move in the right way around the bigger thing.
